meta.description: Deep dive: Nordic/EU market and law

user.t:
READ-ONLY deep research. Fetch and read PRIMARY sources (laws, trade-association terms, official statistics). Do not create or edit files; return text only. Cite URL and date for every claim, and grade A/B/C.

Context: scoup.ai (founder in Norway) is pre-product. Its product is a detention/accessorial recovery agent: evidence packet, demand, deadlines, disputes. It is currently framed for the US market. A first pass found no dedicated Nordic or EU waiting-time recovery vendor, but the legal basis is unclear.
Questions:
1. Norway:
   - Lov om vegfraktavtaler (vegfraktloven): any provisions on waiting time / ventetid, demurrage-like charges, delay?
   - Standard terms used by Norwegian hauliers and forwarders: NSAB 2015, NHO Logistikk og Transport and NLF (Norges Lastebileier-Forbund) standard conditions, Transportbrukernes Fellesorganisasjon. Do they define ventetid, free time and hourly rates (e.g. "ventetid belastes med kr X per påbegynt halvtime etter Y min")?
   - Size of the Norwegian road haulage market: SSB (Statistics Norway) figures on lastebiltransport, number of hauliers, share of small firms.
2. Sweden, Denmark and Finland:
   - the equivalents: Sweden's Allmänna Bestämmelser / Sveriges Åkeriföretag standard terms on väntetid; Danish DTL; Finnish rules.
3. EU:
   - CMR (no waiting-time rule; delay liability capped at the freight charge): confirm.
   - The Mobility Package (driver rest and return rules) and how it raises the cost of waiting.
   - e-CMR adoption status in 2026 (which countries, including Norway's ratification).
   - EU or German/Dutch practice on Standgeld (Germany's HGB §412: Standgeld for waiting beyond loading time). Germany may be the best EU analog: what are the statutory terms?
4. Existing Nordic or EU solutions:
   - waiting-time or standgeld billing apps, forwarder TMS features (e.g. Transporeon/Trimble time-slot management, Alpega, Shippeo, Sixfold, project44 EU, Timocom), and whether any automate claims.
5. Is there a credible "Nordic/EU first" or "Norway pilot" go-to-market?
   - Pros: home market, e-CMR digital evidence, German Standgeld statute.
   - Cons: smaller market, relationship culture, union-negotiated terms.
   - Give an honest verdict versus US-first.
Output ≤ 1000 words, organised by country/topic, with a final "US-first vs Nordic/EU-first" recommendation and its confidence.

handback.t:
NORDIC/EU WAITING-TIME RECOVERY: RESEARCH REPORT (2026-10-10, standard depth, partial)

Process caveats (read first)
- Caller said read-only, so I did NOT write the .claude-flow/research-active.json marker.
- The AIDefence scan tool errored ("package not available"). No fetched text was screened, so screened=false. Treat quotes as unscreened.
- Nothing was stored; acceptance step not applicable.
- Grading: A = primary source read directly. B = primary source read via a summariser, or a reputable secondary source. C = search snippet only, or inferred.
- The WebFetch summariser, not me, read the pages. Lovdata returned 404 and several PDFs were unreadable. Verify every B or C item against the original text before relying on it.

NORWAY
- Vegfraktloven (Act of 20 Dec 2000 no. 107). I could not retrieve the statute text, because lovdata returned 404. Secondary sources only:
  - SNL (https://snl.no/vegfraktloven, 27 Sep 2024) says the carrier is liable for delay unless it cannot be attributed to the carrier. For domestic carriage cargo damage is capped at 17 SDR/kg (8.33 SDR/kg international). The page had no waiting-time rule. Grade B.
  - A search snippet says delay compensation is capped at the freight amount, and that the buyer provides loading and unloading conditions, with separate compensation claimable "unless otherwise agreed". Grade C.
  - I could not confirm any statutory ventetid or demurrage provision. Likely no explicit rule; a claim would rest on the contract or general principles. Unverified.
- NSAB 2015 (https://themis.[REDACTED:high_entropy].html, Danish text). Grade B.
  - The summary found no clauses on waiting time, standing time or demurrage.
  - §19A, §19B and §21B cover delay only, capped at the freight amount.
  - NSAB governs forwarder-to-customer relations, not hauliers' own terms.
- NLF standard terms (lastebil.no "Standardvilkår for transport"): the PDF URL returned 404. I found no verified wording on ventetid, free time or hourly rates. Open question. NHO Logistikk og Transport and Transportbrukernes Fellesorganisasjon: not researched.
- SSB: searches returned only old or irrelevant tables. I did not get current numbers on lastebiltransport firms or the share of small firms. The only figures I have are NLF's own, and they are inconsistent across sources and years (roughly 2,600 to 4,000 members, 15,000 to 25,000 trucks; https://snl.no/Norges_Lastebileier-Forbund). Grade C. Market sizing is unresolved.

SWEDEN / DENMARK / FINLAND
- Sweden: searches surfaced Sveriges Åkeriföretag's "Alltrans 2007" (https://www.akeri.se/media/4duhhndp/alltrans_2007_original.pdf) and NLM 2018 but nothing on väntetid, and I did not open either. Not verified.
- Denmark: the only hit was driver-agreement wage clauses on ventetid, which is employment law, not shipper charges. DTL's figures: ~3,300 members, 20,300 trucks (snippet). The DTL freight terms were not retrieved. Not verified.
- Finland: the finlex fetch returned an image. Not verified.
- Since NSAB 2015 is the shared Nordic forwarder standard and has no waiting-time clause, Nordic waiting-time charges are likely contract- or haulier-terms-driven. That is an inference (Grade C).

EU
- CMR: I did not fetch the text. From my own knowledge, Art. 23(5) caps delay compensation at the carriage charges and the Convention has no waiting-time rule. Grade C because I did not verify it here; confirm at unece.org.
- Germany, HGB §412 (https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/hgb/__412.html, fetched 2026-10-10). Grade B (summarised). Wording as I read it: the shipper must load and unload. No special remuneration is due for the loading and unloading time itself. If the carrier waits beyond that time, by agreement or for reasons outside its risk sphere, it has a claim to "angemessene Vergütung (Standgeld)". There is no statutory rate or time limit.
- German practice (https://www.verkehrsrundschau.de/nachrichten/transport-logistik/standgeld-alles-was-sie-wissen-muessen-3489171, 19 Mar 2024; https://www.eurotransport.de/logistik/spedition-und-logistik/standgeld-anerkannter-ausgleich/):
  - Statute sets no amounts or deadlines, only "angemessen".
  - Snippets say about 2 hours' loading or unloading time is treated as reasonable for a full 40 t load, and EUR 60/hour is accepted in settled case law. Grade C for the figures.
  - BGH case I ZR 37/09 (https://gesetze.co/urteile/I_ZR_37-09) and a VerkehrsRundschau ruling on exceeded loading time slots (standgeld upheld) exist. Not read.
- Mobility Package (Reg. 2020/1054):
  - Weekly rest may not be taken in the cab.
  - Drivers must be able to return home every 3 to 4 weeks.
  - The 8-week vehicle return obligation was annulled by the CJEU in Oct 2024 (https://curia.europa.eu/jcms/upload/docs/application/pdf/2024-10/cp240173en.pdf).
  - Grade B. The mechanism by which this raises the cost of waiting is my inference: scarcer driver hours make idle time more expensive.
- e-CMR: Norway acceded 24 Jun 2020 as the 26th party (https://trans.info/en/norway-ratifies-the-e-cmr-protocol-this-is-the-26th-country-to-rely-on-electronic-transport-documents-189755; Grade B). A vendor page claims 38 parties as of 2025 to 2026, including Austria and Hungary in 2024 and Albania in April 2026 (Grade C; check the UN treaty collection). The Benelux pilot runs until 9 Jul 2027 (https://www.transfollow.com/benelux-pilot-on-ecmr-extended-until-july-2027/). Sweden, Denmark and Finland: the same article says all Scandinavian countries recognise e-CMR (Grade B).

EXISTING SOLUTIONS
- Alpega: Dock Scheduling is claimed to cut carrier wait by up to 50%, and it has a Claims Management module (https://www.alpegagroup.com/en-en/transport-solutions/categories/time-slot-management/). Grade C (vendor marketing).
- Transporeon and Sixfold have merged real-time visibility with the Transporeon platform (https://sixfold.com/news/sixfold-partners-up-with-transporeon-the-largest-logistics-network-in-europe). Grade C.
- I found no evidence of automated Standgeld or detention claims from Transporeon, Alpega, Sixfold, Shippeo, project44 or Timocom. This is absence-of-evidence from a few searches, not a proven gap. Visibility timestamps and gate or dock data are the likely evidence source, so the incumbents are potential partners and also potential competitors.

NORDIC/EU-FIRST VERDICT
- Pros:
  - Germany has a real statutory hook (§412), with settled hourly-rate practice.
  - e-CMR and telematics supply digital evidence.
  - Mobility Package pressure raises the cost of idle drivers.
  - Home-market access in Norway.
- Cons:
  - Norway has no verified statutory waiting-time right, and NSAB is silent. Recovery depends on contract terms.
  - The Norwegian market is small and fragmented (NLF's own figures: thousands of small hauliers) and I could not size it.
  - Claims in Germany need local-language and legal handling, and incumbents (Transporeon/Alpega) sit on the data.
  - I did not verify the relationship-culture or union-terms claim; it is plausible but unevidenced.
- Recommendation: stay US-first for the product. Treat Germany (not Norway) as the first EU test, via a low-cost pilot or design-partner interviews. Do not pivot to a Norway pilot on current evidence. Confidence: low to medium (about 55%), limited by missing SSB, NLF, Swedish and Danish term texts and the unscreened sources.

NEXT STEPS
1. Pull the vegfraktloven text from a working lovdata URL, and the NLF Standardvilkår.
2. Pull SSB tables from the "Næringenes økonomiske utvikling" statistic.
3. Pull NLM 2018 and the DTL terms.
4. Confirm CMR Art. 23(5) and e-CMR parties from UNECE.
5. Interview 5 to 10 German carriers about actual Standgeld collection rates.
